selected.hypothesis: Electrides can be identified by (1) a low average electronegativity and high electronegativity heterogeneity (electropositive, chemically heterogeneous lattice), (2) ambiguous oxidation‑state balance (few plausible assignments), (3) the existence of at least one large interstitial cavity (max clearance), and (4) crystallographic symmetries that favor 0D/1D/2D void networks.

final_fit.note: Model fitted on all labeled structures; probability >= 0.5 means electride. Missing feature values are imputed with the median of these structures.

leaderboard.hypothesis: Electrides can be identified by (1) a low average electronegativity and high electronegativity heterogeneity (electropositive, chemically heterogeneous lattice), (2) ambiguous oxidation‑state balance (few plausible assignments), (3) the existence of at least one large interstitial cavity (max clearance), and (4) crystallographic symmetries that favor 0D/1D/2D void networks.

Electrides can be identified by (1) a low average electronegativity and high electronegativity heterogeneity (electropositive, chemically diverse lattice), (2) a charge‑balance ambiguity reflected by few feasible oxidation‑state assignments, (3) the presence of large and heterogeneous interstitial voids (high mean clearance, large max clearance), (4) crystallographic symmetries that favor void networks, (5) a rich set of interstitial sites approximated by the candidate‑count metric.

Electrides are identified by (1) a highly electropositive and chemically heterogeneous composition, (2) oxidation‑state ambiguity indicating excess electrons, (3) structural symmetries that support interstitial void networks, and (4) sufficiently large and heterogeneous interstitial spaces.

Electrides are distinguished by (1) a low‑average and highly electropositive elemental makeup (low mean electronegativity and a very low minimum electronegativity), (2) the presence of strongly electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth or rare‑earth (f‑block) cations, (3) an open lattice with both large typical interstitial clearance and at least one exceptionally large cavity, (4) oxidation‑state ambiguity that forces excess electrons into voids, and (5) crystal symmetries that favor layered, channel or cage‑type void networks.

Electrides are identified by (1) a low‑average, heterogeneous electronegativity landscape driven by alkali/alkaline‑earth and f‑block cations, (2) a high number of feasible oxidation‑state assignments indicating excess‑electron charge imbalance, (3) an open and heterogeneous interstitial lattice measured by mean clearance and volume per atom, and (4) crystal symmetries (space‑group numbers) that favor cage, channel or layered void networks.

Electrides are identified by a globally electropositive lattice (low mean electronegativity), heterogeneous chemical environments (high electronegativity spread), presence of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth or transition‑metal cations, ample average interstitial clearance, a high number of feasible oxidation‑state assignments indicating charge‑balance ambiguity, and structural motifs (specific space‑groups) that support void networks.

Electrides are identified by a globally electropositive and chemically heterogeneous composition, a rich network of interstitial sites, and sufficiently large typical voids that can host anionic electrons.

Electrides can be identified by a combination of (i) a globally electropositive and chemically heterogeneous composition, (ii) difficulty achieving a charge‑balanced oxidation‑state assignment (excess electrons), (iii) a crystal symmetry that supports void networks, and (iv) sufficiently large and abundant interstitial spaces.
